name: Rebekah and Abraham’s servant
charge: Abraham: making his servant swear to take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites. The servant: asking a sign at the well and worshipping when it came to pass. Rebekah: drawing for the camels, saying, I will go, and covering herself with a vail
summary: Abraham, old and blessed in all things, made the eldest servant of his house swear by the Lord that he would take no wife for Isaac of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred. The servant asked a sign at the well, and before he had done speaking Rebekah came out, gave him drink and drew for all his camels, and he bowed his head and worshipped. Her family inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said she would; when she saw Isaac she lighted off the camel and covered herself with a vail. Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent, and she became his wife, and he loved her.
offenseFull: Abraham was old and well stricken in age, and the Lord had blessed him in all things; he made the eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all he had, swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that he would not take a wife for his son of the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he dwelt, but go to his own country and kindred (Genesis 24:1-4). The Most High never condoned marrying into the other nations; the custom was kept from the beginning, long before Moses wrote the law, and the law states its own reason, that they turn the son away from following the Lord to serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4). Solomon is the prime example: he loved women of the other nations, went after their gods, and had to repent. Tobit says the same to his son: take a wife of the seed of your fathers, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did from the beginning, and their seed shall inherit the land (Tobit 4:12). The forefathers arranged marriages, because the building block of a strong nation is a strong family, and a strong family comes from marriage, not from young people left to their own accord. Abraham told the servant that the Lord God of heaven, who swore to give the land to his seed, would send his angel before him (Genesis 24:7).

At the well the servant prayed for good speed and for kindness to his master, and asked a sign: let the damsel who, being asked to let down her pitcher, answered that she would give his camels drink also be the one appointed for Isaac (Genesis 24:12-14). Before he had done speaking, Rebekah came out, born to Bethuel the son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder, very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: undefiled and beautiful, the kind of wife the forefathers had from the beginning (Genesis 24:15-16). He ran to meet her and asked to drink a little water; she hasted, let down her pitcher and gave him drink, then said she would draw for his camels also, and emptied her pitcher into the trough and ran again to the well (Genesis 24:17-20). She gave a stranger drink and then watered ten camels; that kind and easily entreated spirit is the pattern for the daughters of Israel. When the sign came to pass exactly, the man bowed his head and worshipped, and blessed the God of his master, who had not left him destitute of his mercy and his truth: being in the way, the Lord had led
him to the house of his master’s brethren (Genesis 24:26-27).

Her family asked to keep her ten days, and the servant said not to hinder him, seeing the Lord had prospered his way; so they called Rebekah and inquired at her own mouth whether she would go, and she said, I will go (Genesis 24:55-58). They sent their sister away with her nurse and blessed her: to be the mother of thousands of millions, and that her seed might possess the gate of those which hate them, which is the blessing of Israel and a prophecy (Genesis 24:59-60). Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide, a custom of the forefathers showing the Lord dealt with them long before Sinai (Genesis 24:63). When she saw him she lighted off the camel, and when the servant told her it was his master, she took a vail and covered herself (Genesis 24:64-65). The four mothers covered their heads with actual material as a sign of submission; the power a woman has upon her head is her obedience, the custom the apostle goes into (1 Corinthians 11:5-10).
judgmentFull: The servant told Isaac all things that he had done, and Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her, and he was comforted after his mother’s death, for he received a righteous wife like his mother (Genesis 24:66-67). He was forty when he took her; brothers waiting on a wife can be patient, because the right sister was appointed (Genesis 25:20).

When she was barren, Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, and the Lord was entreated of him, and Rebekah conceived (Genesis 25:21). A barren sister is not to nag her husband but to pray, and a husband is to pray for his wife, because only the Lord opens a womb. The oath against the daughters of Canaan, the sign at the well and the woman who said she would go were all answered inside one house. And the covenant narrows again here: it runs through her children, and of her two sons it is Jacob who carries it.

text.text: And Abraham was old, and well stricken in age: and the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things.
And Abraham said unto his eldest servant of his house, that ruled over all that he had, Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh:
And I will make thee swear by the Lord, the God of heaven, and the God of the earth, that thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell:
But thou shalt go unto my country, and to my kindred, and take a wife unto my son Isaac.
And the servant said unto him, Peradventure the woman will not be willing to follow me unto this land: must I needs bring thy son again unto the land from whence thou camest?
And Abraham said unto him, Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again.

The Lord God of heaven, which took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my kindred, and which spake unto me, and that sware unto me, saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land; he shall send his angel before thee, and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence.
And if the woman will not be willing to follow thee, then thou shalt be clear from this my oath: only bring not my son thither again.
And the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and sware to him concerning that matter.
Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son.
For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and destroy thee suddenly.

Beware of all whoredom, my son, and chiefly take a wife of the seed of thy fathers, and take not a strange woman to wife, which is not of thy father’s tribe: for we are the children of the prophets, Noe, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: remember, my son, that our fathers from the beginning, even that they all married wives of their own kindred, and were blessed in their children, and their seed shall inherit the land.
And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master were in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor.
And he made his camels to kneel down without the city by a well of water at the time of the evening, even the time that women go out to draw water.
And he said, O Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.
Behold, I stand here by the well of water; and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water:

And let it come to pass, that the damsel to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also: let the same be she that thou hast appointed for thy servant Isaac; and thereby shall I know that thou hast shewed kindness unto my master.
And it came to pass, before he had done speaking, that, behold, Rebekah came out, who was born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, with her pitcher upon her shoulder.
And the damsel was very fair to look upon, a virgin, neither had any man known her: and she went down to the well, and filled her pitcher, and came up.
And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher.
And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.
And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.
And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.
And the man wondering at her held his peace, to wit whether the Lord had made his journey prosperous or not.
And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold;
And said, Whose daughter art thou? tell me, I pray thee: is there room in thy father’s house for us to lodge in?
And she said unto him, I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, which she bare unto Nahor.
She said moreover unto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in.
And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the Lord.
And he said, Blessed be the Lord God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the Lord led me to the house of my master’s brethren.
And her brother and her mother said, Let the damsel abide with us a few days, at the least ten; after that she shall go.
And he said unto them, Hinder me not, seeing the Lord hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.
And they said, We will call the damsel, and enquire at her mouth.
And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.
And they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant, and his men.
And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.
And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.
And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.
For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.
But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.
For the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man.
Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man.
For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.
And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.
And they sent away Rebekah their sister, and her nurse, and Abraham’s servant, and his men.
And they blessed Rebekah, and said unto her, Thou art our sister, be thou the mother of thousands of millions, and let thy seed possess the gate of those which hate them.
And Rebekah arose, and her damsels, and they rode upon the camels, and followed the man: and the servant took Rebekah, and went his way.
And Isaac came from the way of the well Lahai–roi; for he dwelt in the south country.
And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide: and he lifted up his eyes, and saw, and, behold, the camels were coming.
And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she lighted off the camel.
For she had said unto the servant, What man is this that walketh in the field to meet us? And the servant had said, It is my master: therefore she took a vail, and covered herself.
And the servant told Isaac all things that he had done.
And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
And Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Padan–aram, the sister to Laban the Syrian.
And Isaac intreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren: and the Lord was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
